questions.text: "___, the warrant linking evidence to claim was never explicitly stated." (most decisive point)
questions.hint: "Crucially" = introducing the most important point

questions.text: "___, not all of the studies were peer-reviewed. Nevertheless, the overall pattern is clear." (concede before countering)
questions.hint: "Admittedly / Granted" = concessive stance adverb

questions.text: "___, the largest studies consistently showed the smallest effect sizes." (counterintuitive finding)
questions.hint: "Surprisingly" = flags a counterintuitive or unexpected result

questions.text: "___ ___ ___ ___ that this correlation has been replicated across multiple independent studies." (impersonal passive)
questions.correct: It has been demonstrated / It has been shown
questions.hint: "It has been demonstrated/shown that + clause"

questions.text: "This ___ raises important questions about the generalisability of the findings." (summary noun = the limitation)
questions.hint: "This limitation" = naming the small sample or narrow context as a limitation

questions.text: "The ___ of these results confirms the central hypothesis." (find → noun, plural)
questions.hint: "find" → "findings" — nominalisation

questions.text: "___ ___ ___ ___ that the assumptions underlying the model require re-examination." (it is significant)
questions.hint: "It is significant that + clause" = impersonal evaluation

questions.text: "___ ___ ___ ___, it can be concluded that both approaches have merit." (given the evidence presented)
questions.hint: "In light of the above" = formal conclusion phrase

questions.text: "___, this represents the most important gap in the current research literature." (contestable claim)
questions.hint: "Arguably" = this can be argued but is not universally agreed

questions.text: "The ___ of the new curriculum took three years." (implement → noun)
questions.hint: "implement" → "implementation" — nominalisation

questions.text: What is the "warrant" in Toulmin's model?
opts: The principle connecting evidence to the claim
The sources cited in the essay
questions.correct: The principle connecting evidence to the claim
questions.hint: Listening 3B: Toulmin model

questions.text: "___ ___ ___ ___ that the intervention has no significant effect on long-term outcomes." (premature to conclude)
opts: It would be premature to conclude
It was premature to have concluded
questions.correct: It would be premature to conclude
questions.hint: "It would be premature to conclude that + clause"

questions.text: "___ ___ ___ that this sample is not representative of the broader population." (it is worth noting)
questions.hint: "It is worth noting that + clause" = comment clause

questions.text: "___ ___ is that both groups showed identical improvement rates." (what is striking)
questions.hint: "What is striking is that + clause" = wh-cleft comment clause

questions.text: What is a "list essay"?
opts: An essay with bullet points instead of paragraphs
An essay with a series of discrete points lacking the argumentative thread connecting them
An essay that lists all sources at the end
An essay with too many body paragraphs
questions.correct: An essay with a series of discrete points lacking the argumentative thread connecting them
questions.hint: Reading 2: "list essay"

questions.text: "___ are an important quality of academic writing — they show intellectual honesty about the limits of claims." (qualifiers)
questions.hint: Listening 3B: "qualifiers are not weakness — they are intellectual honesty"

questions.text: "___ ___ ___ ___ ___ demonstrates a consistent positive effect." (formal: large amount of research)
questions.hint: Replace "loads of research shows" with formal academic expression

questions.text: "Smith and colleagues (2019) ___ that three conditions must be met." (active — specific authors)
questions.hint: Specific authors: active voice "Author(s) argue/demonstrate/find"

questions.text: What distinguishes a strong academic claim from a vague one?
opts: Strong claims are longer and more detailed
Strong claims cannot be contested by anyone
Strong claims are specific, contestable, and require evidence to support
Strong claims quote from high-impact journals
questions.correct: Strong claims are specific, contestable, and require evidence to support
questions.hint: Reading 1: "specific, open to empirical challenge, requires evidence and reasoning"

questions.text: "Participants ___ randomly ___ to one of four conditions." (methods section passive)
questions.hint: Methods: passive voice "were + pp"

questions.text: Which sentence has the strongest academic register?
opts: "Lots of research shows this is true."
"Evidently, a substantial body of peer-reviewed research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach."
"It seems like researchers agree about this."
questions.correct: "Evidently, a substantial body of peer-reviewed research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach."
questions.hint: Stance adverb + formal noun phrase + precise reporting verb = best academic register

questions.text: A reference to a source of information used to support a claim is called a ___.
questions.hint: Reading 1: "proper citation"

questions.text: "This ___ has important implications for language teaching practice." (what the finding is)
questions.hint: "This finding has important implications" = "this + summary noun + verb"

questions.text: "Arguably" should be used before well-established, uncontested facts.
questions.hint: "Arguably" signals contestable claims — not uncontested facts. Use "evidently" for clear evidence.

questions.text: What is "intellectual rigour" in academic writing?
opts: Using very long and complex sentences
Saying exactly what can be supported — no more and no less
Citing as many sources as possible
Writing in a very formal style
questions.correct: Saying exactly what can be supported — no more and no less
questions.hint: Reading 1: "intellectual rigour — saying exactly what can be supported"
